title: Positive Effect of Steroids in Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome
case_prompt:
A 77-year-old woman was referred with acute onset of Broca’s aphasia and right-sided hemiparesis suggestive of a left middle cerebral artery stroke. Her initial blood pressure was 200/110 mm Hg. Noncontrast cranial CT with CT angiography showed no evidence of infarction, hemorrhage, or arterial occlusion. Intravenous thrombolysis with recombinant tissue‐type plasminogen activator was administered, and her blood pressure was immediately and successfully lowered under continuous monitoring. Later that day, she developed a generalized tonic–clonic seizure and was started on intravenous levetiracetam. 

Cerebral MRI performed the next day revealed symmetric bilateral white matter lesions with cortical involvement in the parieto‐occipital lobes and the cerebellum. Diffusion‐weighted sequences remained unremarkable, showing no restricted diffusion. Despite normalized blood pressure and seizure control, her level of consciousness progressively declined to severe impairment. A lumbar puncture revealed mild pleocytosis in the cerebrospinal fluid.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Consideration of acute cerebral infarction was ruled out because “Cranial CT with CT angiography ruled out acute cerebral infarction as well as a cerebral hemorrhage; no arterial vessel occlusions were identified.”  
2. Consideration of intracerebral hemorrhage was excluded by the same imaging findings: “Cranial CT with CT angiography ruled out acute cerebral infarction as well as a cerebral hemorrhage…”  
3. Encephalitis was considered due to inflammatory CSF findings: “In summary of the findings (clinical presentation, MRI, mild pleocytosis in cerebrospinal fluid), two differential diagnoses were considered: PRES or encephalitis.”  
4. Viral encephalitis was excluded when “Viral encephalitis caused by herpes or varicella zoster virus could not be proven, so as a logical consequence the antiviral therapy was stopped immediately.”  
5. Status epilepticus was ruled out by neurophysiological testing: “Status epilepticus was ruled out by serial electroencephalographies.”  
6. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome was supported by the imaging pattern in the setting of hypertension: “MRI revealed symmetric bilateral white matter lesions with cortical involvement in the parieto‐occipital lobe and the cerebellum,” consistent with vasogenic edema.
